paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a sampling method whose effectiveness depends strongly on its hyperparameters. Choosing these settings well matters because the sampler must move toward the distribution of interest efficiently. The paper addresses this tuning problem by changing what the optimization procedure tries to improve.

Existing approaches either optimize a substitute measure for mixing speed or treat the sampling chain as a variational distribution and optimize a tractable lower bound. That bound can be loose in practice. The authors instead propose an objective that directly quantifies convergence speed toward the target distribution and can be optimized using stochastic gradient descent.

The evaluation spans synthetic two-dimensional distributions, sparse signal reconstruction, deep latent variable models, and molecular configurations for a 22-atom molecule. Across these experiments, the method matches or improves on alternative baselines. These findings support the practical value of tuning against a more direct convergence objective across several different sampling tasks, without establishing superiority for every possible target distribution.
icml-2021-a-gradient-based-strategy-for-.tldr: The paper tunes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo using a directly optimized convergence-speed objective, matching or improving on baselines in its experiments.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation asks how a classifier trained in one domain can remain useful in another. This paper studies a model of subpopulation shift in the input space or in a learned representation. Its framework uses a source-domain teacher classifier as a starting point for transferring labels to the target domain.

The mechanism is label propagation through an input consistency loss, which encourages compatible predictions across related inputs. The theoretical analysis relies on an expansion assumption. Under the analyzed conditions, the resulting classifier can transfer predictions to the target domain and improve on the teacher, so propagation need not simply preserve the teacher’s existing errors.

The authors combine their analysis with existing generalization bounds to obtain finite-sample guarantees for deep neural networks. They also extend the framework to transfer supported by an additional unlabeled dataset. Guided by the theory, they adapt consistency-based semi-supervised methods to domain adaptation and report significant improvements. The contribution therefore connects a conditional explanation of successful transfer with practical adaptations of existing learning methods.
icml-2021-a-theory-of-label-propagation-.tldr: Under an expansion assumption, consistency-based label propagation can transfer a teacher’s predictions across domains and improve on the teacher.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization must improve an objective without directly accessing its gradients. This paper considers an especially demanding regime: the decision vector is so large that even basic operations over all its entries are infeasible. In this setting, reducing the number of objective queries alone does not resolve the computational problem.

The proposed method, ZO-BCD, uses zeroth-order block coordinate descent to obtain favorable overall query complexity alongside much lower computation per iteration. The authors also discuss reducing memory use with circulant measurement matrices. These contributions address separate practical constraints: how often the objective is queried, how much work each update requires, and how much information must be stored.

As an application, the paper constructs adversarial examples for neural classifiers in a wavelet representation, producing optimization problems with more than one million dimensions. For audio classifiers, the reported attacks reach a state-of-the-art success rate of 97.9% with significantly less distortion. This application illustrates why computationally manageable updates matter when black-box optimization operates over extremely large representations.
icml-2021-a-zeroth-order-block-coordinat.tldr: ZO-BCD reduces per-iteration computation for enormous black-box optimization problems and supports effective wavelet-domain adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Adding Gaussian noise to neural-network activations is a common regularization technique. The noise can be additive or multiplicative and is introduced during training. This paper examines its implicit effect: how those injections change the behavior of stochastic gradient descent, beyond their role as a regularization procedure.

The authors show that Gaussian activation noise induces asymmetric, heavy-tailed noise in gradient updates. Thus, the distribution of the injected noise does not directly describe the distribution of its consequences for optimization. To study those consequences, they develop a Langevin-like stochastic differential equation driven by a general family of asymmetric heavy-tailed noise.

Within that model, they prove that the injections create an implicit bias whose form depends on both tail heaviness and asymmetry. Experiments across different network types support the proposed description of the training dynamics and find that this implicit effect degrades performance. The findings identify a specific adverse mechanism in the studied settings, rather than establishing that every use of Gaussian noise must reduce overall performance.
icml-2021-asymmetric-heavy-tails-and-imp.tldr: Gaussian activation noise can produce asymmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise, creating an implicit optimization bias that degraded performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering is an unsupervised learning technique, and the paper studies how to perform it while protecting individual privacy. Its central question is how much clustering quality must be sacrificed to obtain differential privacy. The authors assess quality through additive error relative to the optimal clustering cost.

They introduce an algorithm whose additive error grows subquadratically with problem size. This improves on straightforward adaptations of existing non-private algorithms, which produce a trivial quadratic error. The distinction matters because privacy protection is useful only if the resulting quality guarantee still conveys meaningful information about how close the output is to the optimum.

The paper also establishes a fundamental limit: any pure differentially private algorithm for correlation clustering requires additive error of at least linear order in n. This lower bound applies beyond the particular proposed method. Together, the results show that better-than-quadratic error is achievable, while a nonzero and growing privacy-related cost is unavoidable under pure differential privacy.
icml-2021-differentially-private-correla.tldr: The paper achieves subquadratic additive error for private correlation clustering and proves a linear lower bound for pure differential privacy.

paragraphs: Fully supervised learning requires annotations that can be expensive to obtain. Partial labeling offers weaker information: each input comes with a set of possible targets rather than one identified answer. The challenge is to use these candidate sets to learn despite the unresolved ambiguity in individual training examples.

The paper revisits a disambiguation principle for recovering full supervision from weak supervision and turns it into an empirical algorithm. The key task is to resolve which targets the incomplete annotations support, making the information useful for learning. This connects the practical appeal of cheaper annotations with a procedure intended to recover the guidance that complete labels would provide.

Under classical learnability assumptions, the authors prove exponential convergence rates for their algorithm. This is a conditional guarantee about how rapidly the method converges, rather than a claim that arbitrary ambiguous labels can always be resolved. Practical examples illustrate its usefulness. Together, the algorithm and analysis explain how partial labels can support effective learning when the assumed learnability conditions hold.
icml-2021-disambiguation-of-weak-supervi.tldr: The paper proposes an algorithm for disambiguating partial labels and proves exponential convergence under classical learnability assumptions.

paragraphs: Language-transformer activations can be linearly mapped to brain activity during speech comprehension, but those activations combine multiple kinds of linguistic information. This paper develops a way to separate that information so researchers can investigate which aspects of language correspond to different patterns of brain activity.

The authors organize representations along lexical, compositional, syntactic, and semantic categories. They introduce a statistical method that uses GPT-2 activations to decompose fMRI activity from 345 people listening to 4.6 hours of narrated text. The language model serves as a lens for distinguishing linguistic constructs within the recorded activity.

The analysis finds that compositional representations involve a broader cortical network than lexical representations, including temporal, parietal, and prefrontal areas on both sides of the brain. It also suggests that syntax and semantics share a distributed neural substrate rather than occupying separate modules. These findings support studying language through distributed representations, while the framework provides a method for isolating the contributions of different linguistic constructs.
icml-2021-disentangling-syntax-and-seman.tldr: A GPT-2-based analysis of brain activity suggests that syntax and semantics share distributed neural representations.

paragraphs: Riemannian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo traditionally uses the generalized leapfrog integrator to carry out its numerical dynamics. This paper asks whether the implicit midpoint integrator offers a useful alternative. The choice matters because the numerical procedure influences both the cost of sampling and how faithfully it maintains properties needed by the sampler.

The authors discuss theoretical properties and practical advantages and disadvantages of the midpoint approach. Their empirical assessment focuses on energy conservation, volume preservation, and reversibility. Examining these properties separately makes the comparison more informative than simply asking which integrator completes an iteration faster.

The experiments reveal a tradeoff. Leapfrog iterations are faster, but implicit midpoint better conserves energy and consequently achieves higher acceptance rates. It also better preserves volume and reversibility in the reported assessment. The authors argue that these improvements may yield more accurate sampling. The finding therefore supports midpoint as a potentially valuable alternative, while leaving the faster iteration time of leapfrog as a relevant competing advantage.
icml-2021-evaluating-the-implicit-midpoi.tldr: Implicit midpoint trades slower iterations for better empirical conservation properties and higher acceptance rates than generalized leapfrog in Riemannian HMC.

paragraphs: Finite mixture models are often used to estimate how many subpopulations a dataset contains. A common approach places a prior on the number of components and examines its posterior after observing data. Existing consistency results can justify this approach when the assumed component likelihoods exactly match the data-generating process.

The paper examines what happens when that specification is even slightly wrong. Under the developed sufficient conditions, the component-count posterior diverges: as the amount of data grows without bound, the posterior probability of each particular finite component count approaches zero. More observations therefore need not stabilize inference around a meaningful finite number of subpopulations.

The authors also explain that consistency in estimating the overall density is not enough to establish this divergence result. They develop sufficient conditions intended to be more realistic and easier to check than common asymptotic assumptions, and illustrate the consequences using simulated and real data. The work distinguishes accurately representing a distribution from reliably recovering its underlying component count.
icml-2021-finite-mixture-models-do-not-r.tldr: Under the paper’s sufficient conditions, even slight mixture-model misspecification makes posterior probability vanish for every fixed finite component count as data grows.

paragraphs: Designing a protein sequence for a desired three-dimensional fold requires handling a complex relationship between sequence and structure. Multiple sequences can belong to a fold, and capturing that diversity is another challenge. Fold2Seq addresses this task with a transformer-based generative framework conditioned on a target fold.

The framework jointly learns two representations. A transformer embeds protein sequences, while a fold representation describes the density of secondary structural elements within three-dimensional voxels. Learning these representations together is intended to connect sequence information with the target fold, giving the generator a way to use spatial organization when proposing sequences.

With complete, high-resolution structure inputs, experiments show improved or comparable speed, coverage, and reliability relative to existing deep generative methods and RosettaDesign. The advantages become more evident in additional challenges involving low-quality, incomplete, or ambiguous structures. These results support the value of fold-based conditioning when the available structural input is imperfect, as well as its competitiveness on cleaner inputs.
icml-2021-fold2seq-a-joint-sequence-1d-f.tldr: Fold2Seq jointly represents protein sequences and target folds to generate sequences, with particular advantages when structural inputs are imperfect.

paragraphs: Normalization can make neural networks easier to optimize, but methods that work well for one architecture may not transfer directly to another. This paper investigates normalization specifically for graph neural networks. It begins by adapting existing techniques and comparing how they affect training convergence.

InstanceNorm converges faster than BatchNorm and LayerNorm in the reported evaluation. The authors explain this through a preconditioning effect: normalization changes the optimization problem in a helpful way. BatchNorm provides a weaker version of that effect because graph datasets introduce substantial batch noise. However, InstanceNorm has its own problem: its shift operation reduces expressiveness for highly regular graphs.

GraphNorm addresses that expressiveness issue by making the shift learnable. This preserves the motivation for normalization while allowing the model to adjust an operation that could otherwise discard useful distinctions. Empirically, graph neural networks using GraphNorm converge faster than those using other normalization methods and perform better on graph classification benchmarks, indicating benefits for both training and generalization.
icml-2021-graphnorm-a-principled-approac.tldr: GraphNorm uses a learnable shift to address InstanceNorm’s expressiveness problem and empirically improves graph-network convergence and classification performance.

paragraphs: Optimal experimental design can specify a probability distribution over possible measurements, while an actual experiment requires a discrete collection of measurements. Converting between the two is a rounding problem. Existing rounding procedures impose measurement-budget requirements tied to the dimension, which becomes restrictive when that dimension is very large or effectively infinite.

The paper proposes a rounding procedure that removes dimension dependence from the required number of measurements while retaining nearly the same performance guarantees as existing procedures. It also evaluates against an approach that first projects into a lower-dimensional space and then rounds, where the measurement requirement depends on an effective dimension.

The authors use their procedure to develop a kernel-bandit algorithm and report state-of-the-art results for regret minimization and pure exploration. They additionally prove robustness to model misspecification, an advantage over existing UCB-like approaches. The contribution connects a practical obstacle in allocating measurements with improved methods for sequential learning in high-dimensional function spaces.
icml-2021-high-dimensional-experimental-.tldr: A new rounding procedure removes dimension-dependent measurement requirements and enables kernel-bandit algorithms with strong performance and provable misspecification robustness.

paragraphs: Training a classifier usually requires labeling individual examples, which can consume substantial time and labor. This paper studies a weaker form of supervision for binary classification: unlabeled pairs accompanied by confidence information about whether the examples belong to the same class. The training signal describes relationships between examples rather than assigning each one a class.

The authors construct an unbiased estimator of classification risk that can be computed using only this similarity-confidence data. This supplies an objective for learning a discriminative classifier from the available pairwise information. They also show that the estimation-error bound achieves an optimal convergence rate, providing theoretical support for the statistical efficiency of the approach.

Flexible models can still overfit, so the paper adds a risk-correction scheme intended to reduce that problem. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution combines a way to translate similarity confidence into a classification objective with a practical correction for training models that might otherwise exploit the estimator too aggressively.
icml-2021-learning-from-similarity-confi.tldr: The paper learns binary classifiers from pairwise similarity confidence using an unbiased risk estimator and a correction to alleviate overfitting.

paragraphs: Optimization often seeks the best possible action even when a sufficiently good action would meet the practical need. This paper studies Gaussian process bandits under such relaxed criteria. Its central change is to stop penalizing actions once their values are close enough to the optimum or meet a specified threshold.

On the theoretical side, the authors define several forms of lenient regret in which near-optimal actions receive zero penalty. They derive upper bounds for GP-UCB and an elimination algorithm that avoid the usual square-root-of-time term associated with searching extremely close to the maximum. Algorithm-independent lower bounds complement these guarantees by describing limits that are not specific to either method.

For the practical task of finding one acceptable action, the paper introduces algorithms that explicitly use a known threshold. Experiments show that these methods can typically find a good action faster than standard optimization approaches. The findings explain how changing the success criterion can reduce unnecessary search when exact optimization is not required.
icml-2021-lenient-regret-and-good-action.tldr: Treating sufficiently good actions as successful yields improved regret bounds and can speed up finding an acceptable action in Gaussian process bandits.

paragraphs: Removing a training example from a learned model usually requires more than deleting its stored record. DaRE forests modify random forests so that examples can be removed with minimal retraining. Their updates are exact: deleting data produces the same DaRE model as training from scratch on the remaining data.

The design combines randomness with cached information. Upper tree levels use random splits that depend only minimally on the data and rarely need updating. Lower levels choose splits greedily. Statistics stored at nodes and training examples stored at leaves allow the method to update only affected subtrees. For numerical features, greedy splits consider a random subset of thresholds.

The number of random nodes and candidate thresholds provides a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and update efficiency. Across 13 real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset, DaRE forests remove data orders of magnitude faster than full retraining with little or no loss of predictive performance. Exactness concerns the deletion result; the configurable tree design governs the efficiency and prediction tradeoff.
icml-2021-machine-unlearning-for-random-.tldr: DaRE forests combine random splits and caching to delete training examples exactly, achieving much faster updates than retraining in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Feature importance can answer two different questions: what a particular model relies on, or what the data indicate about the contribution of different properties to a phenomenon. This paper focuses on the second question. In that setting, models act as proxies when conducting many real-world experiments is expensive or prohibited.

The authors demonstrate limitations of existing importance scores when they are used to explain data, especially when features are correlated. They then formulate axioms describing properties a score should have for this purpose. Starting from explicit requirements makes it possible to evaluate a score by the behavior it is intended to capture.

They prove that exactly one score satisfies their full set of axioms: Marginal Contribution Feature Importance, or MCI. The paper analyzes its theoretical properties and demonstrates its merits empirically. The uniqueness claim is tied to the proposed axioms, providing a principled basis for this score rather than establishing one universally correct meaning of feature importance.
icml-2021-marginal-contribution-feature-.tldr: MCI uniquely satisfies the paper’s axioms for feature importance aimed at explaining data, addressing problems posed by correlated features.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using observations collected under another policy. Hidden variables can make this difficult when they influence both the environment’s dynamics and the behavior policy’s decisions. The resulting correlations can cause naive estimates to misrepresent the causal effect of using the new policy.

The paper develops worst-case bounds for assessing sensitivity to these unobserved confounders over finite horizons. Its analysis considers confounders drawn independently from the same distribution at each period. Rather than assuming the observed relationships fully identify policy performance, the bounds account for uncertainty caused by hidden influences.

The authors show that a model-based approach using robust Markov decision processes obtains sharper lower bounds by incorporating domain knowledge about the dynamics. They also examine persistent confounders, which remain influential over time. That setting is substantially harder, and existing methods yield extremely conservative bounds. The results show why both knowledge of the system and the temporal structure of hidden variables matter for credible policy evaluation.
icml-2021-model-free-and-model-based-pol.tldr: The paper bounds off-policy evaluation under hidden confounding, showing benefits from dynamics knowledge and greater difficulty when confounders persist over time.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender can influence self-interested receivers by selectively disclosing information. This paper moves to repeated interactions with multiple receivers whose types are unknown and selected adversarially. It considers binary actions and no externalities, and seeks learning algorithms with polynomial computation per iteration.

The results depend on the structure of the sender’s utility. For supermodular or anonymous utilities, the authors establish that polynomial-time no-alpha-regret algorithms are unavailable for any approximation factor alpha between zero and one, including one. For submodular utilities, they instead construct a polynomial-time algorithm with a no-(1-1/e)-regret guarantee. This is an approximation-based regret result, not an unqualified exact no-regret guarantee.

The construction uses a general online gradient descent framework for problems with finitely many possible loss functions. It requires an approximate projection oracle, which the authors show can be implemented in polynomial time for their setting. The paper thereby identifies both computational barriers and a utility structure that permits efficient learning.
icml-2021-multi-receiver-online-bayesian.tldr: For multiple-receiver online persuasion, submodular sender utilities permit efficient approximate no-regret learning, while supermodular or anonymous utilities face impossibility results.

paragraphs: For separable data, regularized logistic regression and support vector machines have a familiar limiting behavior: after renormalization, their estimates approach the maximum-margin classifier as regularization vanishes. This links different learning objectives through a shared geometric solution and helps organize reasoning about generalization.

The paper investigates when that convergence does not hold. It characterizes the behavior through the error distribution in a latent-variable interpretation of linear classifiers. This shifts attention from the apparent similarity of classification methods to the assumptions encoded by their underlying error terms.

In particular, the authors show that regularly varying error distributions prevent the regularized, renormalized estimate from converging to the maximum-margin classifier. This class of heavy-tailed errors therefore produces qualitatively different limiting behavior. The result means that maximum-margin intuition cannot automatically be carried over to such classifiers. The relevant distinction is the modeled error distribution, and the paper argues that this distinction deserves attention when choosing interpretations and methods for real data.
icml-2021-narrow-margins-classification-.tldr: Regularly varying latent errors break the usual convergence of regularized linear classifiers to the maximum-margin solution.

paragraphs: This paper studies fundamental limits on black-box optimization for functions with bounded norm in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The setting can be viewed as a non-Bayesian Gaussian process bandit problem. Its lower bounds describe difficulty inherent to the problem rather than shortcomings of a particular optimization algorithm.

For standard noisy observations, the authors introduce a proof technique that is simpler and more versatile and improves dependence on the allowed error probability. They then consider a robust setting where an adversary perturbs the final selected point. An existing lower bound is strengthened to cover any target success probability strictly between zero and one.

A separate robust setting permits a constrained adversary to perturb every sampled point. Here, the new lower bound applies to deterministic strategies and captures an unavoidable joint dependence of cumulative regret on corruption level and time horizon. This goes beyond bounds that describe those dependencies separately, clarifying how repeated sampling and adversarial interference combine to limit achievable performance.
icml-2021-on-lower-bounds-for-standard-a.tldr: The paper strengthens lower bounds for noisy and adversarially perturbed kernel-bandit optimization, including joint corruption-and-horizon limits for deterministic strategies.

paragraphs: The linear quadratic regulator problem asks how to control a linear dynamical system when costs are fixed quadratic functions. This paper studies learning that control policy online. The central performance question is how regret grows with the time horizon as the learner explores and improves its decisions.

Previously, the optimal dependence on the time horizon had been established only for model-based methods, which require costly system identification. The authors present a model-free algorithm with comparable regret guarantees, achieving square-root dependence on the horizon. This establishes that obtaining that time scaling does not require the model-based route in the studied LQR setting.

The method uses an efficient policy gradient scheme together with a new, tighter analysis of exploration costs in policy space. That analysis matters because trying alternative policies contributes to the cost of learning. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and theoretical: a direct policy-learning procedure and an accounting of exploration sharp enough to support the stated regret guarantee.
icml-2021-online-policy-gradient-for-mod.tldr: An efficient model-free policy gradient method achieves square-root-horizon regret for learning linear quadratic control.

paragraphs: Optimization objectives based on topology appear across data science, statistics, and machine learning. Existing approaches often depend on a particular application or topological construction and lack theoretical guarantees. This paper seeks a common foundation for optimizing functions built around persistent homology.

The authors study differentiability of the persistence map, the central map associated with this topological construction. Using arguments from real analytic geometry, they develop a general framework for defining and computing gradients of persistence-based functions. This makes gradient computation part of a shared mathematical treatment instead of requiring an unrelated solution for each application.

They also give a simple, explicit sufficient condition for convergence of stochastic subgradient methods. The result covers the topological optimization constructions and applications considered in the existing literature, while remaining conditional on that criterion. Accompanying code supports combinations with other methods and constraints, and experiments demonstrate versatility. The work thus connects a general differentiation framework, a convergence guarantee, and tools for incorporating topological objectives into broader optimization tasks.
icml-2021-optimizing-persistent-homology.tldr: The paper provides a general gradient framework for persistence-based objectives and an explicit sufficient condition for stochastic subgradient convergence.

paragraphs: Conditional gradient methods are useful for constrained optimization when projecting onto the feasible set is expensive but optimizing a linear function over it is manageable. They avoid projections, yet generally cannot achieve the globally accelerated rates available to projection-based methods. Local acceleration offers a more attainable improvement in many relevant settings.

An existing locally accelerated conditional gradient method requires knowing the objective’s smoothness and strong convexity parameters. This paper removes that requirement with Parameter-Free Locally Accelerated Conditional Gradients, or PF-LaCG. The change makes local acceleration available without supplying those particular quantities in advance, while preserving rigorous convergence guarantees.

Numerical experiments demonstrate local acceleration and improvements over non-accelerated algorithms in both iteration count and elapsed runtime. These two measures matter together: needing fewer updates is practically useful when it also reduces total computation time. The contribution retains the projection-free motivation of conditional gradients while addressing a parameter-knowledge requirement that limited the earlier acceleration approach. Its acceleration claim remains local rather than global.
icml-2021-parameter-free-locally-acceler.tldr: PF-LaCG achieves local conditional-gradient acceleration without prior knowledge of smoothness and strong convexity parameters.

paragraphs: Following instructions in a changing environment can require more than completing steps in order. An agent may need to revisit a step whose effect has been undone or skip one whose goal is already satisfied. Instructions can also explicitly demand branching and repetition. The paper studies learning both kinds of flexible control flow.

The proposed architecture uses attention over an internal encoding of the instructions. It learns which parts to attend to and how to condition its behavior on them using task reward alone. This allows control to move backward or forward through the instruction sequence as required by the instructions or by changes in the environment.

The authors test the architecture in two illustrative domains inspired by Minecraft and StarCraft. It generalizes without additional training to novel instructions longer than those used during training. Its performance in these tests exceeds that of three recurrent baselines and an ablated architecture. The results support attention as a useful mechanism for learning flexible instruction execution in the evaluated environments.
icml-2021-reinforcement-learning-of-impl.tldr: An attention-based reinforcement learning agent learns to skip and revisit instruction steps and generalizes to longer unseen instructions in two domains.

paragraphs: As autonomous agents take on complicated and potentially risky tasks, checking whether their behavior matches human values becomes important. This paper formalizes value alignment verification as a testing problem. The aim is a compact assessment, analogous to a driver’s test, that verifies alignment using as few queries as possible.

The authors consider both idealized humans with an explicit reward function and humans whose values remain implicit. They analyze exact alignment verification for rational agents and develop heuristics tested in gridworlds and a continuous autonomous driving domain. These settings separate a mathematically explicit version of the problem from more practical testing procedures.

A theoretical result establishes sufficient conditions under which approximate, or epsilon, alignment can be verified in any environment with constant query complexity. The conditions are essential: this is not an unconditional guarantee that a short test certifies every agent. The contribution identifies circumstances permitting efficient verification while also exploring heuristic approaches for settings where practical evaluation is needed.
icml-2021-value-alignment-verification-0.tldr: The paper formalizes efficient alignment testing and proves that sufficient conditions permit constant-query verification of approximate value alignment.
